title: GC generations and collection behavior
description: Understand the generational garbage collection model, how objects move between generations, and what triggers collections at each level.

data.text: The .NET garbage collector organizes the managed heap into three generations. This is not an arbitrary design choice — it is based on a well-tested observation called the generational hypothesis: most objects die young. The vast majority of objects allocated in a .NET program become unreachable within microseconds of being created. By focusing collection effort on generation 0 — the youngest generation — the GC can reclaim large amounts of memory with minimal pause time.

Generation 0 contains the newest objects. Generation 1 is a buffer between the young and old generations. Generation 2 contains long-lived objects — singleton services, cached data, string literals, static references. Objects that survive a collection are promoted to the next older generation. This means a collection of generation 2 is expensive: it scans the entire managed heap, including generations 0, 1, and 2. The GC prefers to avoid full collections whenever possible.

items: **Generation 0** — approximately 256 KB to a few MB. Contains brand-new objects. Collected most frequently. A gen 0 collection typically pauses the application for under 1 millisecond.
**Generation 1** — a buffer of objects that survived one gen 0 collection. About the same size as gen 0. Collected when gen 0 collections fail to free enough space.

**Generation 2** — long-lived objects, including everything promoted from gen 1 and large objects. Can grow to hundreds of MB or more. Full (gen 2) collections are rare but can pause the application for tens of milliseconds.

data.text: The runtime triggers a gen 0 collection when the allocation since the last gen 0 collection exceeds a threshold — typically around 256 KB. If gen 0 collection does not free enough contiguous space for the next allocation, the runtime promotes surviving objects to gen 1 and triggers a gen 1 collection. Gen 1 collection is also triggered when gen 1 reaches a threshold size. Gen 2 collections happen when both gen 0 and gen 1 collections fail to free enough space, or when the system is under memory pressure and the runtime receives a low-memory notification from the OS.

data.title: Observing GC events in real time

data.text: Generations 0 and 1 live together in a region of memory called the ephemeral segment. This segment is typically a few megabytes in size. When the GC collects generation 0, it only needs to scan the ephemeral segment — not the entire managed heap. This is why gen 0 collections are fast. Generation 2 objects live in separate segments called the large object heap and the generation 2 segment. A gen 2 collection must scan all segments, which is why it is slower.

data.caption: Object promotion through the GC generations. Objects that survive collection are promoted; the ephemeral segment contains only generations 0 and 1.

data.title: Large object heap objects skip generations
data.text: Objects larger than 85,000 bytes are allocated directly on the Large Object Heap (LOH) and are treated as generation 2 objects from the moment of allocation. They are never placed in the ephemeral segment and are never collected in a gen 0 or gen 1 collection. Allocating large objects frequently causes full heap collections, which are expensive. Use pooling or slicing to reduce large-object allocations.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: The generational hypothesis holds that most objects die young; the GC exploits this to minimize pause time.
Objects that survive a generation collection are promoted to the next older generation.
The ephemeral segment holds only generations 0 and 1, making gen 0 and gen 1 collections fast.
Objects over 85 KB go directly to the LOH as generation 2, triggering expensive full collections.
